text: GPS satellite clocks gain about 38 microseconds a day on ground clocks: weaker gravity speeds them up more than their orbital speed slows them. Uncorrected, positions would drift about 11 km a day.

In her 1925 thesis Cecilia Payne showed that stars are mostly hydrogen and helium. At Henry Norris Russell's urging she called the result 'almost certainly not real'; four years later he confirmed it.
The Moon is drifting away from Earth by about 3.8 cm a year, measured by bouncing lasers off reflectors left on its surface by Apollo astronauts. Tides are slowly handing it Earth's spin.
"I think I can safely say that nobody understands quantum mechanics." (Richard Feynman, The Character of Physical Law, 1965)
The electrons in a household copper wire drift at well under a millimeter per second. A lamp lights at once because the electromagnetic field, not the electrons themselves, carries the energy.

If the universe were infinite, unchanging and full of stars, every line of sight would end on a star and the night sky would blaze. It is dark largely because the universe has a finite age (Olbers' paradox).
The Sun's core is too cool for protons to overcome their electric repulsion by classical physics. They fuse anyway because quantum tunneling lets them slip through the barrier.
In 1997 Andre Geim levitated a live frog with a powerful magnet, earning a 2000 Ig Nobel Prize. In 2010 he won the Nobel Prize in Physics for graphene, the first person to win both.
A neutron star packs more than the Sun's mass into a ball about 20 km across. A teaspoon of its material would have a mass of over 5 billion metric tons.

In 1911 Heike Kamerlingh Onnes cooled mercury to about 4 kelvin and its electrical resistance vanished: the first superconductor. A current set flowing in a superconducting ring can circulate for years.
The sky is blue because air molecules scatter short wavelengths far more than long ones. It is not violet mainly because sunlight contains less violet and our eyes are less sensitive to it.
About 85 percent of the matter in the universe is dark matter, detected only through its gravity. Decades of experiments have not revealed what it is made of.
About 65 billion neutrinos from the Sun pass through every square centimeter of your body each second. Almost none of them interact with anything.
In 1972 French scientists found that uranium ore at Oklo, Gabon, had run natural nuclear chain reactions about 1.7 billion years ago, on and off for a few hundred thousand years.
Only about 1 percent of a proton's mass comes from the rest masses of its quarks, which the Higgs field provides. Nearly all the rest is the energy of the strong force that binds them.
In 1867 Maxwell imagined a tiny demon sorting fast molecules from slow ones, which seemed to break the second law of thermodynamics. The resolution: erasing the demon's memory must give off heat.
Wings do not lift because air over the top must 'catch up' with air below. That popular explanation is false: air over the top actually reaches the trailing edge first.
"I, at any rate, am convinced that He does not throw dice." (Albert Einstein, letter to Max Born, 1926)
Many bacteria swim with a genuine rotary motor built from proteins. Ions flowing across the cell membrane turn it, spinning the flagellum like a propeller, and it can reverse direction.
On September 14, 2015, LIGO first detected gravitational waves: two black holes of about 36 and 29 solar masses had merged 1.3 billion light-years away, turning about 3 solar masses into wave energy.
A single-junction solar cell in ordinary sunlight can convert at most about 33 percent of the light into electricity, a ceiling calculated by William Shockley and Hans Queisser in 1961.
In 1975 physicist Jack Hetherington listed his Siamese cat, as 'F. D. C. Willard', as co-author of a Physical Review Letters paper, rather than rewrite every 'we' as 'I'.
A lightning bolt heats the air in its channel to about 30,000 kelvin, around five times the temperature of the Sun's visible surface, briefly turning it into plasma.
A black hole's entropy is set by the area of its horizon, not its volume: one quarter of the area in Planck units. This clue inspired the holographic principle.

The quantum Hall effect is topological: a thin electron layer in a strong magnetic field has a Hall resistance locked to h/(ne²), n a whole number, whatever its impurities. It now serves as the standard for resistance.
In 1997 Juan Maldacena conjectured that gravity in a 5-dimensional anti-de Sitter space is exactly equivalent to a quantum theory without gravity on its 4-dimensional boundary. It remains unproven.
Earth's orbit is chaotic: Jacques Laskar found in 1989 that an error of just 15 meters in Earth's position today makes its place in orbit unpredictable beyond about 100 million years.
"It was almost as incredible as if you fired a 15-inch shell at a piece of tissue paper and it came back and hit you." (Ernest Rutherford, on alpha particles bouncing off gold foil, lecture, 1936)
In 2008 lattice QCD, which simulates quarks and gluons on a grid of space-time points, computed the proton's mass from first principles to within about 2 percent.
The Big Bang should have made matter and antimatter in equal amounts, which would have annihilated each other. Yet the universe is made of matter, and nobody knows exactly why.
